title: France
description: The regions that set the templates everyone else adapted, and the appellation system built around place.
L: France created the Appellation d'Origine Contrôlée, AOC, in 1935, after decades of fraud and phylloxera. Today it's called AOP in EU terms, though AOC is still used. Each appellation defines the area, grapes, yields, minimum alcohol and some winemaking. INAO, the national institute, manages them.

Appellations nest from broad to precise. In Burgundy: the regional Bourgogne, then village names like Gevrey-Chambertin, then Premier Cru and Grand Cru vineyards. The smaller the area, the stricter the rules and the higher the expected quality. Below AOP sits IGP, like Pays d'Oc, with looser rules; below that, Vin de France.
Order these Burgundy levels from broadest to most precise.
Each step narrows the area and tightens the rules.

Appellation rules can set maximum yields, minimum ripeness, permitted grapes, planting density and even pruning. They don't usually require grapes to be named on the label, which is why French labels rarely mention them. The idea is that place, not grape, defines the wine.
Rules on grapes, yields and methods
Why do most French labels not name the grape?
The appellation's rules define the grapes, so the place name tells informed drinkers what's in the bottle.
The AOC system, since 1935, ties wine to place with rules
Appellations nest from region to village to vineyard
Rules cover grapes, yields and methods; labels lead with place
Compare Left and Right Bank reds
Name Bordeaux's white and sweet wines

Bordeaux sits on the Garonne and Dordogne rivers, which meet in the Gironde estuary. Its maritime climate is moderate and damp, so vintages vary. The Landes pine forest shields it from Atlantic winds. Red blends dominate, about 85% of production, with Merlot the most planted grape.

On the Left Bank, the Médoc and Graves, gravel soils drain and warm, favouring Cabernet Sauvignon; Pauillac, Margaux and Saint-Julien are the famous villages. On the Right Bank, in Saint-Émilion and Pomerol, cooler clay and limestone favour Merlot and Cabernet Franc. Between the rivers, Entre-Deux-Mers makes mostly dry whites.
Left: Cabernet on gravel. Right: Merlot on clay.
Match each appellation to its bank or area.
Geography shapes the grape mix in each area.

Dry whites blend Sauvignon Blanc and Sémillon; Pessac-Léognan makes the finest, often oaked. Sauternes and Barsac make sweet wines from noble rot, helped by mists from the cool Ciron river. The 1855 classification ranked Médoc reds and Sauternes; Château d'Yquem was given its own top rank.
Sauvignon and Sémillon, dry or sweet
Merlot is the most planted grape in Bordeaux.
Yes. Cabernet Sauvignon is famous on the Left Bank, but Merlot covers more vineyard area across the region.
Bordeaux is maritime, damp and built on blends
The Left Bank favours Cabernet; the Right Bank Merlot
Pessac-Léognan makes fine dry whites; Sauternes sweet ones
Pinot Noir, Chardonnay and the climat
Describe Burgundy's areas from north to south
Explain the climat and the cru hierarchy
Explain how Burgundy's vineyards are owned

Burgundy runs from Chablis in the north, through the Côte d'Or, divided into Côte de Nuits for reds and Côte de Beaune for both colours, then the Côte Chalonnaise, the Mâconnais and, often grouped with it, Beaujolais. The climate is continental, with frost and hail risks. Pinot Noir and Chardonnay are the main grapes.

A climat is a named, precisely bounded vineyard site, recognised by UNESCO since 2015. Burgundy ranks them: 33 Grand Crus, such as Romanée-Conti or Montrachet, at the top, then hundreds of Premier Crus, then village wines. The best sites lie mid-slope, facing east or south-east, on limestone and marl.
Where are Burgundy's best vineyards usually found?
Mid-slope sites have good drainage, sun exposure and soils, and avoid frost pockets.

After the French Revolution, Church land was sold and Napoleonic inheritance laws split vineyards among heirs. The Clos de Vougeot's 50 hectares now have about 80 owners. So a single vineyard name can appear on many labels. Négociants buy grapes or wine from growers and bottle under their own name; domaines bottle their own.
Which statements about Burgundy are true?
Vineyards are often split among many owners
Most wines are blends of many grapes
Burgundy's reds and whites are usually single-variety: Pinot Noir and Chardonnay.
Burgundy runs from Chablis to the Mâconnais
Climats are ranked as Grand Cru, Premier Cru and village
Vineyards are split among many owners; domaines and négociants both bottle
Describe the Loire's four main areas
Explain why Loire wines are fresh

The Loire runs about 1,000 km, with vineyards along much of it. Near the Atlantic, the Pays Nantais makes Muscadet from Melon. Anjou-Saumur makes Chenin Blanc, from dry to sweet, and Cabernet Franc. Touraine makes Vouvray Chenin and Chinon Cabernet Franc. Upstream, the Central Vineyards make Sancerre and Pouilly-Fumé from Sauvignon Blanc.

The Loire is at the northern edge for many grapes. The west is maritime; the Centre is more continental. Cool conditions keep acidity high and alcohol moderate, often 11.5 to 13%. That freshness explains its whites, its sweet wines that never cloy and its sparkling Crémant de Loire and Saumur.
Match each Loire wine to its grape.
Each part of the Loire has its own grape.
Muscadet sur lie, aged on its lees until bottling, is one of the most reliable partners for oysters, and one of France's best bargains.
Why do Loire wines tend to have high acidity?
The Loire is cool, so grapes ripen slowly and keep their acidity.
The Loire has four areas, from Nantais to the Centre
Melon, Chenin Blanc, Cabernet Franc and Sauvignon Blanc lead
A cool climate keeps the wines fresh
Explain its grand cru and sweet wine rules

Alsace lies between the Vosges mountains and the Rhine, on France's border with Germany. The Vosges block rain from the west, so Colmar is one of France's driest cities. Long, sunny, dry autumns let grapes ripen fully. The region switched between France and Germany several times, which shaped its grapes and bottles.
Vosges rain shadow, dry and sunny

Unlike most of France, Alsace labels name the grape. The four noble grapes are Riesling, Gewürztraminer, Pinot Gris and Muscat. Most wines are single-variety and unoaked, or aged in old foudres. Pinot Noir is the only red. Alsace is one of the few French regions that uses a tall, slim bottle called a flûte, by law.
Grapes on the label, tall bottles
Unlike most French regions, Alsace labels usually name the ____.
Alsace names the variety, a habit shared with Germany.

Alsace has 51 Grand Cru vineyards, mostly limited to the four noble grapes. Late harvest wines are labelled Vendanges Tardives; wines from noble rot berries are Sélection de Grains Nobles, with higher minimum sugar. Crémant d'Alsace is France's most produced crémant.
Which are noble grapes of Alsace?
The four noble grapes are Riesling, Gewürztraminer, Pinot Gris and Muscat. Chardonnay is grown in Alsace, mainly for Crémant, but isn't one of them, and Sauvignon Blanc plays almost no role.
Alsace is dry and sunny in the rain shadow of the Vosges
Labels name the grape; Riesling, Gewürztraminer, Pinot Gris and Muscat are noble
51 Grand Crus, plus VT and SGN for late harvest and noble rot
Compare the northern and southern Rhône
Name the main appellations of each
Explain the role of the Mistral

The northern Rhône is narrow and steep, with granite slopes along the river and a continental climate. Syrah is the only red grape, with Viognier, Marsanne and Roussanne for whites. The southern Rhône is wide and Mediterranean, with Grenache leading blends. More than 90% of Rhône wine comes from the south.
North: Syrah, steep. South: Grenache, wide.

The Mistral, a cold, dry northerly wind, blows down the Rhône valley often, sometimes over 90 km/h. It dries vines after rain, reducing disease, but can damage shoots and lower yields. Vines are often planted low or trained against it. Sunny, dry conditions with the Mistral explain why organic farming is common here.
Cold, dry wind that keeps vines healthy
Match each appellation to its main wine.
The north is about single grapes and steep sites; the south about blends.

Côtes du Rhône covers the whole region. Côtes du Rhône Villages, and named villages like Cairanne, are a step up. The crus include Châteauneuf-du-Pape, with its large round stones called galets, Gigondas and Vacqueyras for reds, Tavel for rosé only, and Beaumes-de-Venise for sweet Muscat.
Côtes du Rhône, Villages, then crus
Most Rhône wine comes from the northern Rhône.
Not true. The southern Rhône makes more than 90% of the total. The north is small and steep.
The north grows Syrah on steep granite; the south blends Grenache
The Mistral dries vines and limits disease
Crus include Côte-Rôtie, Hermitage, Châteauneuf-du-Pape and Tavel
Explain their shift from bulk to quality
Name Provence and the south-west's key wines

Languedoc-Roussillon, along the Mediterranean, has about a third of France's vineyards. Once a source of cheap table wine, it now makes characterful blends from Grenache, Syrah, Mourvèdre, Carignan and Cinsault. Hot, dry summers and poor schist and limestone soils suit them. Appellations include Faugères, Saint-Chinian, Pic Saint-Loup and Corbières.

Since the 1980s, growers pulled out high-yielding vines, planted better grapes and restored old Carignan. The IGP Pays d'Oc lets producers make varietal wines, like Chardonnay or Merlot, with fewer rules, a big export success. Roussillon is known for its vins doux naturels, such as Banyuls, Maury and Rivesaltes.
Better grapes, old vines, flexible IGP
What is IGP Pays d'Oc known for?
Pays d'Oc allows producers to label and sell wines by grape, with fewer restrictions than the AOPs.

Provence is the world's reference for pale, dry rosé, mostly from Grenache, Cinsault and Syrah; Bandol makes powerful Mourvèdre reds. The south-west is varied: Cahors for Malbec, Madiran for Tannat, Jurançon for sweet and dry whites, and Bergerac next door to Bordeaux.
Match each appellation to its grape.
The south of France is a patchwork of local grapes.
Languedoc-Roussillon is France's largest vineyard area
It moved from bulk to quality, with IGP Pays d'Oc for varietals
Provence leads rosé; the south-west has Cahors, Madiran and Jurançon
Link grapes to their French homes
Match each region to its main grape.
French labels name the place; knowing the grapes unlocks them.
Which French region usually names the grape on the label?
Alsace names the variety, like Germany.
Bordeaux's Left Bank favours Cabernet Sauvignon on gravel soils.
Yes. Gravel drains and stores heat, helping a late-ripening grape.
Order these Loire areas from the Atlantic inland.
The Loire flows west to the Atlantic; the Central Vineyards are furthest upstream.
AOC rules tie wine to place, with nested levels
The Loire, Alsace and the Rhône each have their own grapes
The south has shifted from bulk to quality, with Provence leading rosé
